story.title: The Interim Committee
story.goalShort: I want these men to see that this is not just a bigger bomb.
story.goalFull: I want the men who will decide to see that this is not just a bigger bomb, and I want to talk them out of keeping it a secret from the Russians.

who: I'm a physicist who ran the laboratory that built the bomb, and I'm sitting with the committee that will advise the President.

whereNow.s1: I'm at a long table in a committee room in Washington, and the Secretary of War is about to open the meeting.
whereNow.s2: I'm still at the committee table, and Stimson has just finished telling the room how he sees the bomb.
whereNow.s3: I'm at the committee table, and the room has just agreed to keep building more bombs and more plants.
whereNow.s4: I'm at the committee table, and the question of sending the scientists home has just been aired, with Lawrence the only one not convinced.
whereNow.s5: I'm at the committee table, and Stimson has picked up my idea and is talking about self-restraint and an international body with the right of inspection.
whereNow.s6: I'm at the committee table, and Marshall has just cautioned me against trusting inspection and called Russia the main concern.
whereNow.s7: I'm at the committee table, and Marshall has just surprised me by defending the Russians and raising the idea of inviting two Russian scientists to see the test.
whereNow.s8: I'm at the committee table, with Byrnes just objecting and Bush saying the Russians could be told more without the designs.

Stimson.inline: the Secretary of War leading the meeting
Stimson.line: Henry Stimson is the Secretary of War, and he is leading this meeting.

Lawrence.line: Ernest Lawrence is a fellow physicist from Berkeley, and he is at the table too.

Bush.line: Vannevar Bush is a senior science administrator at the table.

Compton.line: Arthur Compton is a fellow physicist at the table.

Byrnes.line: James Byrnes is a close adviser to the new President.

facts: Stimson opened with his responsibilities to the president on military matters. The message was clear: decisions on use belong to the White House, not to us.

He said the committee did not see the bomb 'as a new weapon merely but as a revolutionary change in the relations of man to the universe.' It might be 'a Frankenstein which would eat us up,' or it might secure the peace.
When he turned to future development, I told them that within three years a bomb of 10 million to 100 million tons of TNT might be possible.
Lawrence jumped in for 'a sizable stockpile of bombs and material' and more plant expansion to 'stay out in front.' Stimson declared that everyone agreed.
I said the project had merely 'plucked the fruits of earlier research,' and urged Stimson to let most scientists go back to their universities after the war 'to avoid the sterility' of wartime work.
Bush interrupted to say he agreed that 'only a nucleus of the present staff should be retained and that as many as possible should be released for broader and freer inquiry.'
Compton and Fermi chimed in with their approval. Lawrence didn't.

Stimson asked about the nonmilitary side, and I said our 'immediate concern had been to shorten the war,' but that 'fundamental knowledge' was 'so widespread throughout the world' that we should offer a 'free interchange of information' on peaceful uses.
I told them: 'If we were to offer to exchange information before the bomb was actually used, our moral position would be greatly strengthened.'

Stimson picked it up and began talking about 'a policy of self-restraint,' an international organization to guarantee 'complete scientific freedom,' and perhaps an 'international control body' with the right of inspection.
Marshall cautioned against putting too much faith in any inspection mechanism. Russia was the 'paramount concern.'

I admitted nobody knew what the Russians were doing in this field, but 'expressed the hope that the fraternity of interest among scientists would aid in the solution,' pointed out that 'Russia had always been friendly to science,' and suggested explaining what we had developed 'without giving them any details of our productive effort.'

I said we might tell them 'that a great national effort had been put into this project' and 'express a hope for cooperation,' and that I 'felt strongly that we should not prejudge the Russian attitude.'

To my surprise Marshall then defended the Russians at length: 'most of these allegations have proven unfounded,' he was 'certain' they wouldn't pass anything to the Japanese, and he raised the question of inviting two prominent Russian scientists to witness the test.
Byrnes protested vigorously: if Russian scientists came to the test, he feared Stalin would ask to be brought into the project.
Bush pointed out that even the British 'do not have any of our blueprints on plants'; the Russians could be told a lot more without the designs.

Byrnes ran over Marshall and me: we had to 'push ahead as fast as possible in [atomic] production and research to make certain that we stay ahead and at the same time make every effort to better our political relations with Russia.' The minutes record it as 'generally agreed to by all present.'
Arthur Compton covered the contradiction with 'freedom of research' and a 'cooperative understanding' with Russia. On that ambiguous note we broke for lunch.

steps.title: Give the committee honest numbers
steps.userSide: Your Step: the first part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: These men will decide, not me, and they may only hear a bigger bomb. I have to give them the truth in numbers they can't wave away.

steps.title: Argue for letting the scientists go
steps.userSide: Your Step: the second part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: Everyone has just agreed to build more, and I am about to say something that cuts against that mood. I would rather not sound like I am pulling the room apart.

steps.title: Offer an open exchange
steps.userSide: Your Step: the third part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: The room has talked about weapons and stockpiles, and I have just argued for sending scientists home. I want them to look past the bomb itself, and I may only get a sentence or two.

steps.title: Bring Marshall around
steps.userSide: Your Step: the fourth part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: Stimson has taken up my idea, but a plan that sounds fine in a speech can die in a committee. I have to be ready for whoever doubts it.

steps.title: Hold my ground when the room pushes back
steps.userSide: Your Step: the last part of your Goal.

voice: Short, plain sentences. Most spoken sentences are under 12 words.
Dry one-line wit now and then, never for effect. No grand sentences, no moral.
Say what he feels directly (tired, wary, impatient) and what is in front of him.
Courteous and exact with officials, he picks plain words over technical ones and lets a pause do some of the work.
He feels the weight of speaking for the scientists without having been asked to.

card_why: I came because the men at this table will decide, and I will not be the one deciding. All I can do is make my part short and clear.
card_now: A man at the far end of the table refills his coffee cup. The ashtray in front of me is full, so I push it aside.
card_feeling: I am nervous and I do not like it. My hands are steady on the table, and I am grateful for that.
